subject: biology-hl
about: Original practice questions written for NevaIB from the IB guide's syllabus understandings and the school's unit order. Not IB past-paper questions, not publisher material and not IB markschemes: the marking points are written for self-marking. Organisms, experiments and data in data-response items are invented for practice.

choices: A hexose sugar, a phosphate group and a nitrogen-containing amino acid
A pentose sugar, a fatty acid and a nitrogenous base
A pentose sugar, a phosphate group and a nitrogenous base
Glycerol, a phosphate group and a nitrogenous base
items.note: Nucleotides are the monomers of DNA and RNA. Phosphate links to the sugar of the next nucleotide.

items.stem: Which base is found in RNA but not in DNA?
choices: Uracil
Thymine
Adenine
Guanine
items.note: RNA has A, U, C, G; DNA has A, T, C, G.

items.stem: In DNA, the two strands are held together by:
choices: Covalent bonds between the sugars
Hydrogen bonds between complementary bases
Ionic bonds between phosphate groups
Peptide bonds between the bases
items.note: A–T and C–G pair by hydrogen bonds; the backbone of each strand is held by covalent bonds.

items.stem: A DNA sample contains 22% adenine. What percentage is cytosine?
Which is a difference between DNA and RNA?
choices: DNA is single-stranded; RNA is double-stranded
DNA contains uracil; RNA contains thymine
DNA contains deoxyribose; RNA contains ribose
DNA has phosphate; RNA has none
items.note: DNA: deoxyribose, double helix, thymine. RNA: ribose, usually single strand, uracil.

items.stem: The sugar–phosphate backbone of a nucleic acid strand is formed by:
choices: Hydrogen bonds between the hydroxyl groups of neighbouring deoxyribose sugars along the same strand
Covalent bonds between the phosphate of one nucleotide and the sugar of the next
Covalent bonds between neighbouring bases
Ionic bonds between neighbouring phosphates
items.note: Condensation reactions link nucleotides into a strong backbone, with bases projecting to one side.

items.stem: DNA can store a huge amount of information because:
choices: The sequence of its four bases can vary without limit along the molecule
It contains twenty different bases
Its sugar–phosphate backbone varies in each gene
Each nucleotide carries a different amino acid
items.note: Information is in the base sequence; any sequence is possible, so the number of combinations is enormous.

items.stem: The two strands of DNA are antiparallel, which means:
choices: Both strands run 5′→3′ in the same direction
The strands are twisted in opposite directions
One strand is DNA and the other RNA
One runs 5′→3′ and the other 3′→5′
items.note: The 5′ end (phosphate) of one strand is opposite the 3′ end (OH) of the other.

items.stem: Purines always pair with pyrimidines because:
choices: Purines and pyrimidines have the same number of rings
One two-ring base plus one single-ring base gives a constant helix width
Purines can only form one hydrogen bond
Pyrimidines are larger than purines
items.note: A and G are purines (two rings); C and T are pyrimidines (one ring). A purine–pyrimidine pair fits the helix exactly.

items.stem: The Hershey–Chase experiment showed that DNA is the genetic material because:
choices: Radioactive sulfur in the viral protein coats was found inside the infected bacteria after the viruses were removed
Viruses without DNA could still infect bacteria
DNA was found in larger amounts than protein in viruses
Radioactive phosphorus (in DNA) entered bacteria, but radioactive sulfur (in protein) did not
items.note: ³²P labels DNA, ³⁵S labels protein. Only the ³²P was found in infected bacteria and passed to new viruses.

items.stem: Nucleosomes help to package DNA in eukaryotes. Each consists of:
choices: DNA wrapped around a core of eight histone proteins
RNA wrapped around a core of DNA polymerase
A single histone wrapped around a loop of RNA
A ring of DNA in the cytoplasm of a bacterium
items.note: DNA coils around histone octamers like beads on a string, condensing it and helping regulate gene expression.

markscheme: Double helix of two antiparallel polynucleotide strands (1)
Sugar–phosphate backbone with bases pointing inward (1)
Complementary base pairing A–T, C–G by hydrogen bonds (1)
items.tactic: Outline = key features, not the full detail.

items.stem: Compare the structure of DNA and RNA.
markscheme: Both are polymers of nucleotides with a sugar–phosphate backbone (1)
DNA has deoxyribose; RNA has ribose (1)
DNA has thymine; RNA has uracil (1)
DNA is double-stranded; RNA is usually single-stranded (1)
items.tactic: At least one similarity and three paired differences.

items.stem: Explain how Chargaff's data helped falsify the tetranucleotide hypothesis.
markscheme: The hypothesis said DNA had a repeating unit of the four bases in equal amounts (1)
Chargaff found base proportions differed between species (1)
But A = T and C = G in each species (1)
Unequal proportions meant DNA could vary enough to carry information (1)
items.tactic: Falsification: state the prediction, the data, and why they conflict.

items.stem:
(Invented data for practice.) Base composition (%) of DNA from four invented organisms: P A 30, T 30, G 20, C 20; Q A 18, T 18, G 32, C 32; R A 25, T 15, G 35, C 25; S A 26, T 26, G 24, C 24.
(a) Identify the organism whose DNA is likely to be single-stranded, with a reason. (b) Calculate the ratio (A+T)/(G+C) for organism Q. (c) Suggest why DNA from Q would need a higher temperature to separate its strands than DNA from P.
markscheme: (a) R, because A ≠ T and G ≠ C, so bases are not paired (1)
G–C pairs have three hydrogen bonds (A–T has two), so more energy is needed to separate the strands (1)
items.tactic: Unfamiliar context: find the syllabus idea being tested, quote the data (with units) when you describe a trend, then explain it with that idea. One marking point per linked step.
